claims.text: Atomic size mismatch induced by composition produces local lattice distortion in high-entropy alloys.
HEA nanoparticles in the proposed 5–50 nm range are homogeneous while intrinsically lattice-distorted because they contain atoms of different sizes.
Systematic compositional tuning can vary atomic size mismatch and lattice distortion while preserving nearly identical surface composition.
Increasing atomic size mismatch increases local lattice strain and distortion.
The degree of lattice distortion can be quantified through local strain fields and bond-length variations.
Local lattice strain caused by atomic size mismatch reduces the energy barrier for atomic mobility at nanoparticle surfaces.
The reduced mobility barrier enhances surface atomic mobility.
Enhanced surface mobility causes premelting or surface disorder to begin at a lower temperature.
Earlier premelting facilitates faster progression to complete melting and lowers the full-melting temperature.
Nanoparticles with greater lattice distortion will have a lower premelting onset temperature than minimally distorted baseline nanoparticles.
Nanoparticles with greater lattice distortion will progress to complete melting more rapidly than the baseline.
Minimizing atomic size mismatch will reduce lattice distortion in the baseline nanoparticles.
The proposed mechanism applies to HEA nanoparticles from 5 to 50 nm under inert or vacuum heating from near room temperature through complete melting.
Residual surface segregation may occur despite efforts to control surface composition.
A lack of a significant melting difference or correlation with measured distortion would falsify lattice distortion as the primary governing factor.
